result: LPS + PA (LP) treatment induces lysosomal Ca2+ release in macrophages, evidenced by reduced perilysosomal Ca2+ release by GPN and decreased [Ca2+]Lys measurements, leading to increased cytosolic Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i).
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C22, and C23 are well-supported by multiple complementary measurements including GCaMP3-ML1 imaging showing reduced GPN-induced perilysosomal Ca2+ release (Figure 1A), OGBD measurements showing decreased [Ca2+]Lys (Figure 1B), and Fluo-3-AM/Fura-2 measurements showing increased [Ca2+]i (Figure 1C). The inference that reduced GPN response indicates lysosomal Ca2+ depletion is reasonable and supported by citations to similar findings.

result: BAPTA-AM, a Ca2+ chelator, abrogates IL-1β release and maturation by LP without affecting pro-IL-1β levels, demonstrating that increased [Ca2+]i is functionally required for inflammasome activation.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by ELISA data showing BAPTA-AM reduces IL-1β release (Figure 1D) and immunoblotting showing reduced mature IL-1β without affecting pro-IL-1β levels (Figure 1E). The inference that BAPTA-AM's effect is unrelated to transcription/translation inhibition is reasonable given unchanged pro-IL-1β levels.

result: LP induces synergistic ROS accumulation, particularly mitochondrial ROS, which is functionally required for inflammasome activation and [Ca2+]i increase, as demonstrated by NAC and MitoTEMPOL inhibition experiments.
evaluation: Claims C28-C36 are well-supported by CM-H2DCFDA fluorescence showing LP induces more ROS than PA or LPS alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), MitoSOX data showing mitochondrial ROS accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and functional data showing NAC and MitoTEMPOL reduce both [Ca2+]i and IL-1β release (Figures 1E, 1F, 1—figure supplement 1B, 1—figure supplement 1C). The synergistic effect inference is reasonable.

result: TRPM2 is expressed on lysosomes of BMDMs and participates in LP-induced inflammasome through ADPR-mediated activation, as demonstrated by colocalization studies and inhibition by CD38 inhibitors (apigenin, quercetin).
evaluation: Claims C37-C44 are supported by immunofluorescence showing TRPM2-LAMP2 colocalization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), ELISA data showing apigenin/quercetin reduce IL-1β release (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and Ca2+ imaging showing these inhibitors reduce [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C). The mechanism involving ADPR is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

result: Trpm2 knockout abrogates LP-induced [Ca2+]i increase, [Ca2+]Lys decrease, and inflammasome activation without affecting ROS production, indicating TRPM2 acts downstream of ROS in lysosomal Ca2+ release.
evaluation: Claims C45-C52 are well-supported by comprehensive data showing Trpm2-KO prevents [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 2A), [Ca2+]Lys decrease (Figure 2B), IL-1β release (Figure 2C), and ASC speck formation (Figure 2D), while not affecting ROS production (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D). The inference that TRPM2 is downstream of ROS is logical.

result: Trpm2 knockout inhibits inflammasome activation by lysosomotropic agents (LLOMe, MSU) but not by nigericin or ATP, indicating TRPM2 is specifically crucial for inflammasome involving lysosomal Ca2+.
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by ELISA data showing differential effects of Trpm2 KO on different inflammasome activators (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). The selectivity for lysosomotropic agents versus plasma membrane-acting agents (nigericin, ATP) provides strong evidence for lysosomal TRPM2 specificity.

result: Trpm2 knockout ameliorates HFD-induced metabolic inflammation and glucose intolerance in mice, with reduced blood glucose, improved IPGTT, reduced HOMA-IR, and decreased inflammasome markers (ASC specks, caspase-1 cleavage, CLS) in adipose tissue.
evaluation: Claims C58-C67 are comprehensively supported by in vivo data including blood glucose measurements (Figure 3A), IPGTT with AUC (Figure 3B), HOMA-IR calculations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), histological analysis of CLS (Figure 3C), ASC speck quantification (Figure 3D), and caspase-1 cleavage (Figure 3E). Body weight was controlled (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).

result: LP does not activate plasma membrane TRPM2 current, as shown by patch clamp studies with ACA and cyclic ADPR, and bafilomycin A1 experiments demonstrate that lysosomal TRPM2 is the primary mediator of LP-induced [Ca2+]i increase.
evaluation: Claims C68-C76 are supported by whole-cell patch clamp data showing LP does not affect plasma membrane TRPM2 current amplitude or basal activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C), and bafilomycin A1 experiments showing that lysosomal Ca2+ depletion prevents TRPM2-dependent [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). This provides strong evidence for lysosomal versus plasma membrane TRPM2.

result: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurs after LP-induced lysosomal Ca2+ release, as demonstrated by simultaneous monitoring showing [Ca2+]ER decrease paralleling [Ca2+]Lys recovery in Ca2+-free conditions.
evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are well-supported by GEM-CEPIA1er and D1ER measurements showing [Ca2+]ER decrease after LP treatment in Ca2+-free medium (Figure 4A), and simultaneous monitoring showing inverse relationship between [Ca2+]ER and [Ca2+]Lys during recovery (Figure 4B). The temporal correlation provides strong evidence for ER→lysosome Ca2+ flux.

result: ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling occurs through IP3R channels (not RyR), as demonstrated by Xestospongin C and TPEN inhibition of [Ca2+]Lys recovery, and this refilling contributes functionally to inflammasome activation.
evaluation: Claims C82-C88 are supported by OGBD measurements showing Xestospongin C (IP3R inhibitor) and TPEN (ER Ca2+ chelator) prevent [Ca2+]Lys recovery while dantrolene (RyR inhibitor) does not (Figure 4C), and ELISA data showing Xestospongin C reduces IL-1β release (Figure 4D). The channel specificity and functional relevance are well-demonstrated.

result: LP induces ER-lysosome membrane contact sites, as shown by increased VAPA-ORP1L proximity ligation assay signals, which may facilitate ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling.
evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by PLA data showing increased VAPA-ORP1L contacts after LP treatment (Figure 4E). The inference that these contacts facilitate Ca2+ refilling is reasonable and supported by citation to Yang et al., 2019, though the mechanistic link is not directly tested.

result: Store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE) is activated during LP-induced inflammasome to replenish ER Ca2+ stores, as demonstrated by EGTA, 2-APB, and BTP2 inhibition of inflammasome, and BTP2 reduction of [Ca2+]ER in LP-treated cells.
evaluation: Claims C91-C98 are well-supported by ELISA data showing EGTA, 2-APB, and BTP2 reduce IL-1β release (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, C), and D1ER measurements showing BTP2 reduces [Ca2+]ER in LP-treated cells when extracellular Ca2+ is present (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). The functional role of SOCE is clearly demonstrated.

result: SOCE occurs through ORAI1 channels in LP-induced inflammasome, as evidenced by STIM1 aggregation and colocalization with ORAI1 after LP treatment.
evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by confocal microscopy showing STIM1 puncta formation and colocalization with ORAI1 after LP treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E). These are established hallmarks of SOCE activation, and the inference is well-supported by citation to Vaca, 2010.

result: K+ efflux is coupled to SOCE in LP-induced inflammasome, as demonstrated by high extracellular K+ inhibiting inflammasome, reducing [Ca2+]ER, impairing [Ca2+]Lys recovery, and suppressing [Ca2+]i increase.
evaluation: Claims C102-C109 are comprehensively supported by Potassium Green-2-AM showing [K+]i decrease (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), ELISA showing high [K+]e inhibits inflammasome (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), D1ER showing high [K+]e reduces [Ca2+]ER (Figure 5A), OGBD showing impaired [Ca2+]Lys recovery (Figure 5B), and Fluo-3-AM showing suppressed [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 5C). The coupling is well-demonstrated.

result: Ca2+-activated K+ channels, specifically KCa3.1 (not BK or SK channels, and not other K+ channels), mediate K+ efflux in LP-induced inflammasome, as shown by selective inhibitor studies.
evaluation: Claims C110-C119 are well-supported by systematic pharmacological profiling showing charybdotoxin (pan-Ca2+-activated K+ channel inhibitor) and TRAM-34 (specific KCa3.1 inhibitor) reduce IL-1β release, while inhibitors of BK, SK, and other K+ channels do not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D). The selectivity for KCa3.1 is clearly demonstrated.

result: KCa3.1 channel facilitates Ca2+ influx after ER Ca2+ emptying and mediates K+ efflux during inflammasome, as shown by TRAM-34 revealing [Ca2+]ER decrease, inhibiting [Ca2+]i increase, and preventing [K+]i decrease.
evaluation: Claims C120-C125 are supported by D1ER measurements showing TRAM-34 reveals [Ca2+]ER depletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), Fluo-3-AM/Fura-2 showing TRAM-34 reduces [Ca2+]i increase (Figure 5D), and Potassium Green-2-AM showing TRAM-34 prevents [K+]i decrease (Figure 5E). The positive role of KCa3.1 in Ca2+ influx is well-demonstrated.

result: BTP2 (SOCE inhibitor) suppresses both [Ca2+]i increase and [K+]i decrease by LP, likely by preventing Ca2+ influx that would activate KCa3.1 channels.
evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by Fluo-3-AM/Fura-2 and Potassium Green-2-AM measurements showing BTP2 prevents both Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux (Figure 5D, E). The inference that SOCE inhibition prevents KCa3.1 activation is logical and consistent with Ca2+-activated channel biology.

result: LP increases KCa3.1 channel activity without increasing Kcnn4 expression, as demonstrated by nystatin-perforated patch clamp showing increased TRAM-34-sensitive current and RT-PCR showing unchanged Kcnn4 mRNA.
evaluation: Claims C129-C133 are well-supported by nystatin-perforated patch clamp data showing increased TRAM-34-sensitive slope conductance after LP treatment (Figure 6A, B), RT-PCR showing no change in Kcnn4 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and validation in Kcnn4-KO cells showing no TRAM-34-sensitive current (Figure 6C, D). The technique validation strengthens the findings.

result: Kcnn4 knockout significantly reduces IL-1β release and inflammasome activation by LP, prevents [K+]i decrease, but does not affect TNF-α or IL-6 release, demonstrating KCa3.1 channel specificity for inflammasome.
evaluation: Claims C134-C139 are supported by ELISA and immunoblotting showing reduced IL-1β release and caspase-1 cleavage in Kcnn4-KO cells (Figure 6E), Potassium Green-2-AM showing no [K+]i decrease (Figure 6F), and ELISA showing unchanged TNF-α/IL-6 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C). The specificity for inflammasome versus other inflammatory responses is well-demonstrated.

result: K+ efflux through KCa3.1 contributes to [Ca2+]Lys recovery after LP removal, likely through facilitation of SOCE and subsequent ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling, as shown by TRAM-34 inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C140-C141 are supported by OGBD measurements showing TRAM-34 prevents [Ca2+]Lys recovery after LP removal (Figure 6G). The mechanistic inference linking K+ efflux to SOCE facilitation and ER→lysosome refilling is logical and consistent with the established coupling between these processes.

result: LP induces physical association between KCNN4 and ORAI1 channels in a Ca2+-dependent manner, which may facilitate functional coupling between K+ efflux and SOCE.
evaluation: Claims C142-C145 are supported by PLA data showing increased KCNN4-ORAI1 contacts after LP treatment that are prevented by BAPTA-AM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D). However, the functional significance (claim C143) is speculative and only supported by citation, not direct experimental evidence. The Ca2+-dependence is well-demonstrated.

result: Kcnn4 knockout inhibits inflammasome by lysosomotropic agents (LLOMe, MSU) but not by nigericin or ATP, indicating KCa3.1 channel is specifically crucial for K+ efflux associated with lysosomal Ca2+ channels.
evaluation: Claims C146-C150 are supported by ELISA data showing differential effects of Kcnn4 KO on different inflammasome activators (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E). The selectivity pattern mirrors that of Trpm2 KO, providing strong evidence for the lysosomal Ca2+-KCa3.1 axis specificity.

result: KCa3.1 channel is required for NLRP3 oligomerization and NLRP3-NEK7 binding in LP-induced inflammasome, as shown by Kcnn4 knockout or TRAM-34 treatment abrogating these interactions.
evaluation: Claims C151-C154 are supported by BN-PAGE showing reduced NLRP3 oligomers in Kcnn4-KO cells (Figure 6H) and immunoprecipitation showing reduced NLRP3-NEK7 binding with Kcnn4 KO or TRAM-34 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, G). This links KCa3.1 to the core inflammasome assembly mechanism.

result: Kcnn4 knockout ameliorates HFD-induced metabolic inflammation in mice, with improved glucose tolerance and reduced inflammasome markers (caspase-1 cleavage, ASC specks, CLS) in adipose tissue.
evaluation: Claims C155-C158 are comprehensively supported by in vivo data including IPGTT showing improved glucose tolerance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H), immunoblotting showing reduced caspase-1 cleavage (Figure 6I), immunofluorescence showing fewer ASC specks (Figure 6J), and histology showing fewer CLS (Figure 6K). This validates the in vitro findings in a disease-relevant model.

result: LP induces delayed JNK activation at 21 hr (distinct from early transient JNK activation by LPS alone at 30 min), suggesting different mechanisms depending on additional events such as lysosomal Ca2+ release.
evaluation: Claims C159-C162 are supported by time-course immunoblotting showing biphasic JNK activation: early transient activation by LPS alone and delayed sustained activation by LP at 21 hr (Figure 7A). The inference of different mechanisms is reasonable given the distinct temporal patterns.

result: At 21 hr after LP treatment, [Ca2+]i, K+ efflux, and ER Ca2+ depletion are more pronounced than at 4 hr, suggesting full alteration of intracellular Ca2+ distribution occurs at later time points.
evaluation: Claims C163-C167 are supported by time-course measurements showing higher [Ca2+]i (Fluo-3-AM), lower [K+]i (Potassium Green-2-AM), and reduced [Ca2+]ER (D1ER) at 21 hr compared to 4 hr (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). This temporal progression is consistent with the delayed inflammasome activation.

result: ASC phosphorylation and oligomerization occur at 21 hr after LP treatment (but not at 0.5 hr after LPS alone despite similar JNK activation), indicating that delayed JNK activation with signal 2 (lysosomal events) is required.
evaluation: Claims C168-C170 are supported by immunoblotting showing ASC phosphorylation (Figure 7B) and DSS crosslinking showing ASC oligomerization (Figure 7C) only at 21 hr after LP, not at 0.5 hr after LPS despite similar JNK activation levels. This demonstrates that JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient, requiring additional signals.

result: Delayed JNK activation by LP at 21 hr is suppressed by Kcnn4 or Trpm2 knockout, indicating that lysosomal Ca2+ release and/or K+ efflux are necessary for this delayed activation.
evaluation: Claims C171-C173 are supported by immunoblotting showing reduced JNK phosphorylation in both Kcnn4-KO and Trpm2-KO cells treated with LP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). This links the lysosomal Ca2+-K+ efflux axis to delayed JNK activation.

result: JNK activation is necessary but not sufficient for ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization and inflammasome, as shown by SP600125 (JNK inhibitor) suppressing these events and the lack of ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization at 0.5 hr after LPS despite JNK activation.
evaluation: Claims C174-C177 are supported by immunoblotting and DSS crosslinking showing SP600125 reduces ASC phosphorylation and oligomerization (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), ELISA showing reduced IL-1β release (Figure 7E), and the temporal dissociation between JNK activation and ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization (Figures 7B, C). The necessity but insufficiency is well-demonstrated.

result: ASK1 (not TAK1) mediates delayed JNK activation in LP-induced inflammasome, as shown by selonsertib (ASK1 inhibitor) but not 5Z-7-oxozeaenol (TAK1 inhibitor) reducing IL-1β release and JNK activation, with ASK1 activation observed at later time points.
evaluation: Claims C178-C183 are supported by ELISA showing selonsertib but not 5Z-7-oxozeaenol reduces IL-1β release (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), immunoblotting showing selonsertib reduces JNK phosphorylation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), and time-course showing ASK1 activation at later time points (Figure 7A). The pathway specificity is well-demonstrated.

result: Activated ASK1 induces JNK activation and subsequent ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, as shown by ASK1 inhibitor blocking these events as efficiently as JNK inhibitor.
evaluation: Claims C184-C185 are supported by DSS crosslinking and immunoblotting showing selonsertib reduces ASC oligomerization and phosphorylation comparably to SP600125 (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C). This establishes ASK1 as upstream of JNK in this pathway.

result: CaMKII mediates ASK1 activation by LP, as shown by KN-93 (CaMKII inhibitor) but not KN-92 (inactive analog) attenuating ASK1 activation, supporting roles of increased [Ca2+]i and CaMKII in ASK1 activation.
evaluation: Claims C186-C188 are supported by immunoblotting showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduces ASK1 phosphorylation (Figure 7F). The use of the inactive analog KN-92 as a control strengthens the conclusion that CaMKII specifically mediates this effect. The mechanism is supported by citation to Okada et al., 2014.

result: CaMKII inhibition by KN-93 (but not KN-92) inhibits JNK phosphorylation, IL-1β maturation, and IL-1β release by LP, linking increased [Ca2+]i to inflammasome activation through the CaMKII-ASK1-JNK pathway.
evaluation: Claims C189-C191 are supported by immunoblotting showing KN-93 but not KN-92 reduces JNK phosphorylation and mature IL-1β (Figures 7F, G), and ELISA showing reduced IL-1β release (Figure 7H). This completes the mechanistic pathway from Ca2+ to inflammasome activation.

result: The complete mechanistic pathway: increased [Ca2+]i due to lysosomal Ca2+ release (facilitated by ER→lysosome Ca2+ refilling and K+ efflux through KCa3.1 channel) induces delayed activation of ASK1 and JNK, leading to ASC oligomerization, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and metabolic inflammation.
evaluation: Claim C192 represents the integrated conclusion from all preceding results. It is well-supported by the comprehensive data showing: (1) lysosomal Ca2+ release through TRPM2, (2) ER→lysosome refilling through IP3R, (3) SOCE activation, (4) K+ efflux through KCa3.1 coupled to SOCE, (5) CaMKII-ASK1-JNK pathway activation, (6) ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization, and (7) in vivo validation in HFD models. The mechanistic pathway is coherent and well-supported.
